rationale: The entry's core identification — bread as the word of God — is directly carried by the cited texts. Deuteronomy 8:3 and Matthew 4:4 pair bread with 'every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God' as the true sustenance of man, and Matthew 16:12 is Jesus's own explicit decoding of the leaven-of-bread figure as doctrine ('he bade them not beware of the leaven of bread, but of the doctrine of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees'). Given that key, the printed elaborations follow with small steps: leavened bread contains corrupting doctrine (Matt 16:12), and unleavened bread is pure doctrine (1 Cor 5:7-8, 'the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth,' with Ex 12:15 and Lev 2:11 supplying the legal pattern that leaven must be purged from what is offered to and eaten before God). The strongest counter — the mainstream christological/eucharistic reading that bread is Christ himself or his body — does not materially deny this core: Christ is the Word (John 1), John 6:63 grounds the flesh-eating discourse in 'the words that I speak unto you,' and the common interpretation itself lists the word-of-God sense as a standard complementary layer of the same multivalent symbol, not a rival referent. Against the specific texts the entry actually prints, the word-of-God identification with the leaven mechanic is the better-fitting explanation, since the eucharistic reading has no account of Matt 16:12's doctrine-key or the leavened/unleavened polarity.
book_core_identification: Bread symbolizes the word of God (divine teaching/doctrine) as the true sustenance by which man lives.
book_secondary_elaborations: Leavened bread symbolizes doctrine containing corruption.
chapter_only_objections: The claim that widows, orphans, strangers, and the poor symbolically denote the covenant people themselves is a chapter-level application not asserted in the entry.
The identification of the garment as the righteous deeds of the saints and 'to clothe is to grant righteous deeds' is chapter material.
The reinterpretation of 'the poor' as the bowed/humble rather than the materially poor (camel-and-needle argument) is chapter material.
The equation 'to feed is to teach the commandments' (Feed my sheep, meat in due season) is a chapter inference beyond the glossary entry.
The chapter's handling of John 6 ('His body is the bread, the word to be eaten') extends the entry into eucharistic territory not printed in the entry.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Bread primarily symbolizes Jesus Christ himself — the 'Bread of Life' — and his body given for believers in the Eucharist (John 6:35, 48-58; Matt 26:26; 1 Cor 11:23-26), with manna as the type; the word-of-God sense (Deut 8:3; Matt 4:4) and the leaven-as-corruption sense (Matt 16:12; 1 Cor 5:7-8) are complementary secondary layers of the same symbol.
counter_core_identification: Bread = Christ himself / the body of Christ as divine life-giving sustenance.
material_core_denial: No material denial exists. The counter identifies bread with Christ, but Christ is himself the Word of God (John 1:1, 14), and John 6:63 explicitly resolves the bread-of-life discourse into Jesus's words ('the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life'). Both identifications can be true of the same referent; indeed every supplied common-interpretation response lists the word-of-God sense as a recognized layer of the bread symbol, not a rival to it. The counter is a broader, christologically framed statement of the same sustenance-by-divine-word core, so it does not defeat the entry.
counter_case: John 6:35, 48-58 has Jesus say 'I am the bread of life' — an identification with a person, not merely with teaching.
Matt 26:26 / 1 Cor 11:23-26 identify the broken bread with 'my body,' the institutional center of Christian bread symbolism.
The manna typology (Ex 16; John 6:31-33) is read across all major traditions as foreshadowing Christ, not merely doctrine.
Ecclesial consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions makes the christological/eucharistic sense the dominant reading, with word-of-God as secondary.
book_explanatory_advantages: Matthew 16:12 is an in-text authorial key: Jesus himself decodes leaven-in-bread as doctrine, which the eucharistic reading cannot use and the entry is built on.
Deut 8:3 / Matt 4:4 state the bread-word substitution outright: man lives not by bread but by God's word — the exact equation the entry prints.

The leavened/unleavened polarity (Ex 12:15; Lev 2:11; 1 Cor 5:7-8) is coherent only if bread is something that can be pure or corrupted in content — doctrine fits; a body-of-Christ referent has no natural corrupted counterpart.
1 Cor 5:8 explicitly names unleavened bread 'sincerity and truth,' matching 'pure doctrine.'

The word-of-God reading absorbs the christological texts without strain (Christ is the Word; John 6:63), whereas the eucharistic reading leaves Matt 16:12's doctrine-key and Amos 8:11's word-famine motif unexplained as bread mechanics.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Directly explains the Last Supper institution texts and John 6's first-person identification ('I am the bread of life').
Matches the dominant historical consensus across Christian traditions.
Explains the manna typology as pointing to a person who came down from heaven.
decisive_sources: Matthew 16:12 — Jesus's explicit decoding of the leaven of bread as doctrine, the hinge for both printed elaborations.
Deuteronomy 8:3 with Matthew 4:4 — the scriptural bread/word equation stated in both Testaments.
1 Corinthians 5:7-8 — unleavened bread defined as sincerity and truth, old leaven as corruption to be purged.
Exodus 12:15 and Leviticus 24:5-9 pattern via Leviticus 2:11 — the legal exclusion of leaven grounding the purity polarity.
unresolved_objections: 1 Cor 5:8's leaven is glossed as 'malice and wickedness' — moral conduct as well as doctrine — so the entry's strictly doctrinal framing of the leaven polarity slightly narrows Paul's usage, though Matt 16:12's explicit doctrine-key keeps the printed assertion supported.
The entry does not itself address the Last Supper / John 6 institution texts; its harmony with them depends on the Christ-as-Word identification, which is standard but not printed in the entry.
